title: Grade XI Physics — Unit 3 Translatory Motion — FBISE-Style Descriptive Practice
scope: Unit 3 only; 40-mark descriptive practice, not an official full-syllabus FBISE examination
source: NBF Grade XI Physics Unit 3 pp.33–52; supplied FBISE HSSC-I Physics Assessment Framework and 50% model paper, Sections B and C
assessmentPolicy: Summative theory SLOs P-11-B-04, B-05, B-06, B-12, B-13 only; exclude formative P-11-B-03 and B-11. Internal OR alternatives are both assigned their complete mark allocation. Suggested markings are author-created teaching guidance, not official board examiner allocations.
teacherInstructions: Credit equivalent correct scientific reasoning, alternative valid derivations, coherent signs and units. Marks are awarded for demonstrated steps; do not double award. These step allocations are suggestions requiring teacher approval.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from textbook Short Question 3.2; free fall pp. 36–37
choices.prompt: A ball is thrown vertically upward. With upward chosen positive, state its velocity and acceleration at the highest point and explain why the acceleration is not zero.

marking.text: At the highest point the instantaneous vertical velocity is zero.
Gravity continues acting downward, so acceleration has magnitude g ≈ 9.8 m/s².
With upward positive, a = −g = −9.8 m/s².
Changing velocity rather than nonzero velocity is what acceleration describes; the ball begins descending after the instant at the top.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Original constant-acceleration summative application; concept pp. 33–36
choices.prompt: A car slows uniformly from 20 m/s to rest in 5 s. Calculate its signed acceleration and the displacement while braking, taking forward as positive.

marking.text: Given u = +20 m/s, v = 0, t = 5 s.
Use s = (u+v)t/2 or s = ut + ½at².
s = (20+0)(5)/2 = +50 m. The negative acceleration is deceleration, not negative displacement.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from textbook Short Question 3.4(a); horizontal-launch pp. 38–39
choices.prompt: An object is launched horizontally from a height with no air resistance. Describe the horizontal and vertical components of its initial velocity and acceleration, and write the position equations after time t (take downward positive).

marking.text: Initial horizontal component vₓ(0) = u; initial vertical component vᵧ(0) = 0.
Horizontal acceleration aₓ = 0 and vertical acceleration aᵧ = +g (downward-positive).
Horizontal displacement x = ut.
Downward vertical displacement y = ½gt²; the components develop independently.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from textbook equal-range discussion pp. 40–42
choices.prompt: For a projectile launched and landing at equal height with no air resistance, explain why launch angles 30° and 60° produce the same range at fixed launch speed, and state one property that differs.

marking.text: For equal launch/landing heights, range R = u²sin(2θ)/g.
At θ = 30°, the range factor is sin60°.
At θ = 60°, sin120° = sin60°, giving equal ranges.
Time of flight and maximum height are generally different (60° gives greater values than 30°).

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Original example based on textbook range equation p.41
choices.prompt: A projectile leaves ground at 20 m/s at 45° and lands at its starting height. Neglect air resistance and use g = 10 m/s². Calculate its range and time of flight.

marking.text: Identify u = 20 m/s, θ = 45°, g = 10 m/s², equal start/end level.
R = u²sin(2θ)/g.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from textbook Short Question 3.4(b); angled launch pp.39–41
choices.prompt: At three positions of an ideal projectile launched upward at an angle—ascending, highest point, and descending—describe the directions of velocity and acceleration. Explain the horizontal component of velocity.

marking.text: Ascending: velocity points upward and forward; acceleration is downward due to gravity.
At highest point: vertical velocity is zero but horizontal velocity is nonzero; acceleration is downward.
Descending: velocity points downward and forward; acceleration remains downward.
With no air resistance, horizontal velocity is constant because aₓ = 0.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from textbook Short Question 3.6 and Figure 3.6(b), p.42
choices.prompt: Explain four qualitative ways air resistance alters a projectile's motion compared with an otherwise identical ideal launch.

marking.text: Air resistance opposes the instantaneous velocity; it is not a constant downward force.
It generally decreases the forward horizontal velocity, whereas ideal vₓ is constant.
It changes vertical acceleration: drag acts downward during ascent and upward during descent.
Maximum height and horizontal range are generally smaller than in the no-drag model.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Original summative qualitative scenario based on textbook Figure 3.6(b), p.42
choices.prompt: A projectile travels through still air. Explain the direction of air resistance during ascent and descent, and why the ideal equal-range property for complementary angles need not hold.

marking.text: Resistive drag acts opposite the instantaneous velocity.
During ascent, the vertical drag component points downward, adding to gravity.
During descent, the vertical drag component points upward, opposing gravity.
The symmetry R(θ) = R(90°−θ) assumes no drag; drag changes component motions and does not generally preserve the equal-range result.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from textbook Comprehensive Question 3.3 / Section 3.4.1 p.47
choices.prompt: For an isolated head-on elastic collision, state the two conservation laws and the relation between the relative speeds of approach and separation.

marking.text: Total linear momentum is conserved: m₁u₁+m₂u₂=m₁v₁+m₂v₂.
Total kinetic energy is conserved: ½m₁u₁²+½m₂u₂²=½m₁v₁²+½m₂v₂².
Relative approach speed = u₁−u₂ (for approaching configuration and signed velocities).
Relative separation speed = v₂−v₁, so u₁−u₂ = v₂−v₁ for the ideal elastic collision.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from equal-mass collision special case, textbook p.48
choices.prompt: Two equal-mass balls collide elastically head-on. Ball 1 moves at +6 m/s while ball 2 is initially at rest. Determine their final velocities and explain the result.

marking.text: Set m₁=m₂=m, u₁=+6 m/s, u₂=0.
In a 1D head-on elastic collision of equal masses, the bodies exchange their velocities.
Thus v₁ = 0 m/s and v₂ = +6 m/s.
Momentum and kinetic energy remain conserved; an explicit valid check or explanation earns credit.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.prompt: A 0.5 kg ball travelling to the right at +4 m/s collides elastically head-on with a stationary 3.5 kg ball. Find both final velocities.

marking.text: Given m₁=0.5 kg, m₂=3.5 kg, u₁=+4 m/s, u₂=0; use isolated 1D elastic collision formulas.
Interpret v₁ negative as rebound and include the correct signs/units or conservation check.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from textbook Comprehensive Question 3.6 / inelastic collisions p.46
choices.prompt: Explain why total momentum may stay conserved in an isolated inelastic collision even though total kinetic energy decreases. Give examples of forms receiving the lost kinetic energy.

marking.text: In an isolated system the net external impulse is zero, so total momentum is conserved.
An inelastic collision does not conserve total kinetic energy as kinetic energy.
Some initial kinetic energy converts into deformation, internal/thermal energy and/or sound.
Total energy is not destroyed; distinguish conversion from loss of total energy (or provide a correct example).

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Original inelastic collision numerical application based on p.46
choices.prompt: A 4 kg object travelling at +3 m/s sticks to a stationary 2 kg object. Determine the common velocity and the reduction in total kinetic energy of the isolated pair.

marking.text: Momentum: p = 4(3)+2(0) =12 kg·m/s, giving shared v =12/(4+2)=+2 m/s.
Initial K = ½(4)(3²) = 18 J.
Final K = ½(6)(2²) =12 J.
Decrease in kinetic energy =18−12=6 J, transferred into other forms.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from textbook Comprehensive Question 3.5, pp.40–41
choices.prompt: For an ideal projectile launched at speed u and angle θ above level ground and landing at the same height, derive formulas for maximum height, time of flight and horizontal range.

marking.text: Resolve initial velocity: uₓ=u cosθ, uᵧ=u sinθ; horizontal acceleration is zero, vertical acceleration −g.
At highest point vᵧ=0: 0=(u sinθ)²−2gH.
Hence maximum height H=u²sin²θ/(2g).
For return to original level: 0=(u sinθ)T−½gT²; nonzero T=2u sinθ/g.
Horizontal range R=(u cosθ)T.
Substitute T and use sin2θ=2sinθcosθ to give R=u²sin(2θ)/g.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from horizontal-launch description pp.38–39 and end Numerical 3.5, p.52
choices.prompt: A ball rolls horizontally off a cliff of height 45.2 m and lands 17.6 m from its base. Neglect air resistance. Calculate (a) time to land, (b) initial horizontal speed and (c) final downward vertical speed. Use g=9.8 m/s².

marking.text: Set downward positive: uᵧ=0, h=45.2 m and h=½gt².
Horizontal x=uₓt with constant uₓ.
Vertical speed at landing vᵧ=gt.
vᵧ≈9.8×3.04≈29.8 m/s downward.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Adapted from textbook Comprehensive Question 3.3 and elastic-collision section p.47
choices.prompt: Show from conservation of momentum and kinetic energy that, in a nontrivial isolated one-dimensional elastic collision, relative speed of approach equals relative speed of separation.

marking.text: Write momentum conservation m₁u₁+m₂u₂=m₁v₁+m₂v₂.
Rearrange to m₁(u₁−v₁)=m₂(v₂−u₂).
Write kinetic energy conservation m₁u₁²+m₂u₂²=m₁v₁²+m₂v₂².
Factor to obtain m₁(u₁−v₁)(u₁+v₁)=m₂(v₂−u₂)(v₂+u₂).
Divide by the nonzero momentum-factor equation: u₁+v₁=v₂+u₂.
Therefore u₁−u₂=v₂−v₁, which equates relative approach and separation speeds for the head-on elastic collision.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.

choices.sourceRef: Original comparison extension based on inelastic collision section p.46 and textbook Example 3.7 pp.48–49
choices.prompt: A 5 kg body travelling at +10 m/s collides with a 10 kg body travelling at +5 m/s. Compare total momentum and total kinetic energy before impact with the result if the bodies stick together. Explain why this differs from an elastic collision.

marking.text: Initial total momentum p=5(10)+10(5)=100 kg·m/s.
For sticking, common v=100/(5+10)=+6.67 m/s.
Initial kinetic energy Kᵢ=½(5)(10²)+½(10)(5²)=375 J.
After sticking, K𝒇=½(15)(100/15)²≈333.33 J.
Kinetic-energy reduction =375−333.33≈41.67 J; isolated-system momentum remains 100 kg·m/s.
Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy; in sticking collisions some kinetic energy becomes deformation, heat or sound.

choices.notes: Accept equivalent correct physics, equations, signs, units and mathematically consistent rounding.
